doc.title: Roswell Rudd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Call and response; Ayler, Taylor, Murray and Worrell
summary: Rudd teaches call and response and describes hearing a Greenwich Village quartet of Ayler, Cecil Taylor, Sunny Murray and Lewis Worrell in 1961.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: In listening to the little bit I just heard you play in the other room, I noticed two things that I thought really stuck out for me, and that was you seem to be creating melodies with some patterns in them, that you were building upon what you had just played, and that you also felt that a space now and then in your solo was important.
That’s not playing would set up something to play next, or as an answer to something you had played, to put a space there.

Yeah. The call-response is the thing that I teach right at the beginning. And the idea with this is that it’s better to wait if an idea doesn’t come right away. And then you have the advantage of being with one, two, three, four other, five other people. And this is a great chance for some kind of dialogue to happen. And this to me is basic in the music. If I don’t hear the call and response and the music never has a chance to breathe, it eliminates one of the great ways that I have of getting into it. If I hear the call and response going down, if I hear the talking going back and forth you know, players acknowledging to each other that they hear what they’re doing, I hear you and here’s what I say back. When I hear the give and take I’m in there right away. When I don’t hear the give and take, I have to look for something else to grab on to. But the give and take gives me an automatic way, a wonderful, easy way in there. So even though I’ve say heard some pretty wild little bands, for instance here’s a wild little band, Albert Ayler on the tenor and soprano saxophones with Cecil Taylor on the piano, Sunny Murray on the drums and Louis Worrell on the bass, playing together in a coffee house in Greenwich Village in 1961 or something. They’re talking. They’re talking. Yeah. And otherwise I probably wouldn’t have been able to get into that, you know, because the sound is like this to me. It was a lot of sound, probably more sound than I’d ever heard from such a little band before. But they were, even though they were filling the space, they were communicating © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-
